activities.caption: place the system on the century scale
activities.name: kpLinnaeusPlace

config.prompt: The binomial system arrived in 1753 — place it on the century scale:
config.why: Carl Linnaeus, 1753: genus capitalised, species not, both italicised — unique worldwide and in any language, which is exactly what common names fail at.

activities.caption: pair each family with its prediction
activities.name: kpFamilyMatch

config.prompt: Families are predictive — pair each group with what the name tells you:

pairs.right: four-petalled flowers — and cabbage white butterflies and clubroot across every member, kale to wallflowers
shared flower structure, pruning timing and disease susceptibilities
tomatoes and potatoes that share diseases
the species name that says medicinal

config.why: Learn the major horticultural families and a plant's name starts reading like a care sheet — the full ladder has seven rungs, but gardeners work mostly in the bottom three.

activities.anchor: Flowering plants fall into two great groups
activities.caption: file each trait under monocot or dicot
activities.name: kpMonoDicotBuckets

config.prompt: The deepest practical split — file each trait:

items.label: vascular bundles scattered through the stem
vascular bundles arranged in a ring

config.why: One seed leaf or two? It decides vein patterns and root architecture — and which herbicide works, since many are selectivity tricks.

activities.anchor: grass is not built like a shrub
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the mowing myth
activities.name: kpMowSpot

config.prompt: One line of this mowing summary is wrong — click it:
lines: Grass's growing points sit at the base, below the mower blade.
A mown blade is not a wound to heal but a leaf that regrows from the base.
Grass is, in effect, built to be grazed.
The lower you cut, the better — grass regrows from the base however much you remove.
What hurts is cutting too low at once.
config.correction: Cutting too low at once is exactly what hurts — the plant runs short of leaf to photosynthesise with. Leave at least two-thirds of the blade.
config.why: Monocots grow from the base, dicots from tips and cambium — which is why mowing works on one and pruning shapes the other.

activities.anchor: a wilted lettuce is a turgor problem
activities.caption: drag the divider — one vacuole, two states
activities.name: kpTurgorCompare

config.prompt: The central vacuole, before and after — drag the divider:

before.label: Turgid
before.text: Full of stored water; the pressure inside keeps soft tissue firm.

after.label: Wilted
after.text: Pressure gone — watering revives the plant, but it cannot fix disease the same way.

config.why: The vacuole is one of three features animal cells lack, with the cellulose cell wall (wood is essentially walls, thickened with lignin) and the chloroplast, which converts light, water and carbon dioxide into sugar and oxygen.

activities.anchor: Two transport tissues run through all of this
activities.caption: file each job under its tissue
activities.name: kpTransportBuckets

config.prompt: The plumbing and the pores — file each job:

items.label: conducts water and minerals upward from the roots
powered largely by the pull of evaporation from the leaves — the cohesion–tension mechanism
conducts sugars from where they are made to where they are used or stored
why a branch fed by its own leaves fruits well
why defoliating a tree starves its roots
adjustable pores mainly on leaf undersides
carbon dioxide enters and water vapour exits here

config.why: The epidermis seals surfaces with a waxy cuticle — and the stomata are the plant's thermostat, the link between watering, wilting and ventilation.

activities.anchor: most feeder roots are shallow and fine
activities.caption: water the tree — make the calls
activities.name: kpRootsBranch

config.root: July, and a young tree is stressed. Where should the water go — and how often?

start.text: Remember the root–shoot division of labour.

choices.label: A little and often, at the trunk
choices.feedback: Water occupies only the top few centimetres — roots stay shallow and the plant collapses in the first hot, dry spell.

choices.label: Deeply and less often, out at the drip line
choices.feedback: Roots chase the moisture downward — the plant you wanted.

choices.label: Daily misting over the leaves
choices.feedback: Plants drink from their roots, not their leaves — and wet leaves overnight can promote fungal disease.

sips.text: Shallow roots, then a dry spell: a disaster trained by kindness.

deep.text: Feeder roots run shallow and fine, and they respire from soil air — compaction kills them by squeezing that air out. Root damage costs more than shoot damage: shoots regrow from buds, roots regrow slowly.

mist.text: Foliar feeding is a supplement, not a substitute. If you remember one thing about watering, remember the roots.

config.why: Roots anchor, absorb through the fine root hairs, and often store — carrots, dahlia clusters — and every watering can in the shed is a tool for managing that job.

activities.anchor: a solitary apple tree fruits poorly
activities.caption: bet before you read on — the lonely tree
activities.name: kpApplePredict

config.q: A lone apple tree crops badly year after year. Why?
choices: It exhausted its soil in the first season
Most apples need cross-pollination from a different variety
Apples fruit only on old spurs, and a young tree has none
config.why: Pollination and fertilisation produce seeds, and fruit production is managed by knowing what pollinated what — which is also why some cucumbers set fruit without pollen at all.
